stories.headline: Chris Fagan to join the Blues as director of coaching in 2027
stories.summary: Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.
stories.body:
Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.

The 65-year-old stepped down as Brisbane's senior coach after the club's 2026 premiership win -- it's third in a row -- with an aim to return closer to family.

Announced by the Blues on Saturday morning, Fagan will oversee a matchday role and begin mentoring the coaching panel to "establish development pathways for the coaches and help drive an elite, sustainable football program".

Fagan said he was looking forward to making a "real impact" at the Blues.

"While I loved my 10 years as a Senior Coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said in a statement.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting. I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be.

"In all my conversations with [the club] before accepting the role, what resonated strongly was how aligned they were on how to make Carlton a great football club. They shared a clear vision of evolving Carlton into a club that can contend but most importantly, they understand there is still significant work to do to get there.

"To have the senior leadership of a football club share such clarity in their direction, combined with a role that gives me genuine purpose, makes joining Carlton an opportunity too good to pass up."

Meanwhile Carlton's GM of Football Chris Davies said the appointment was an important one to support first-time senior coach Josh Fraser.

"We want to build our football club around good people and they do not come any better than Chris Fagan," Davies said.

"Few in the game have his wealth of experience and ability to connect with and get the best out of those around him. Most importantly, he is a proven winner who knows what it takes to build a consistently high-performing environment.

"Chris and Josh have built a connection in recent weeks over a shared philosophy of putting people first and building a program the right way. With Chris on board, Josh will be well supported, our coaches will be well developed and our program will continue to build the clarity and discipline required to be truly elite.

"We can't wait to welcome Chris and his wife Ursula, their daughters Jessica and Ellen and the entire Fagan family to Carlton."

...more to come.

stories.headline: Ponga back for NZ as Walsh wins Aussie fullback role
stories.summary: Australian coach Kevin Walters has shown his hand with a big fullback call as New Zealand superstar Kayln Ponga returns for the Rugby League World Cup semis.
stories.body:
Kayln Ponga and Reece Walsh are on track to resume their compelling rivalry after two huge coach calls ahead of the Rugby League World Cup semifinals.

Ponga has been named on New Zealand's extended bench for Saturday night's do-or-die showdown with Tonga in Newcastle, just 22 days after breaking his forearm in a dazzling fullback duel with Walsh in the tournament opener.

And Walsh on Tuesday retained the Australian No.1 jumper ahead of James Tedesco for the Kangaroos' semi-final against Samoa in Sydney on Sunday.

While young gun Keono Kini will again start as custodian at McDonald Jones Stadium, Ponga's inclusion is a firm indication the Newcastle Knights superstar will return for the final should the Kiwis make it.

Coach Stacey Jones also selected hooker Phoenix Crossland among the Kiwis' extended reserves as Australian Test coach Kevin Walters made the most significant move of his tenure by picking Walsh over Tedesco.

The selection dilemma has bubbled along through Australia's three group-stage wins.

Tedesco entered the World Cup in exceptional form after helping the Sydney Roosters to the NRL premiership, while Walsh had spent the last two months on the sidelines with an ankle injury.

But Walsh - the star of last year's Ashes series - has done enough to win the backing of former Broncos coach Walters for the business end of the tournament.

Walsh and Ponga were both electrifying in Australia's 24-22 win over New Zealand last month, before Walsh was man of the match with a hand in five tries in last Saturday's 66-6 rout of the Cook Islands.

In other key Australian selections, Bradman Best has made the left centre spot his own by seeing off the challenge of South Sydney talisman Latrell Mitchell.

Tedesco and Mitchell are both part of a six-man bench that includes Canberra's Ethan Strange and Cameron Murray for the likely Allianz Stadium sell-out.

Tom Dearden and Cameron Munster will line up together in the halves.

"Samoa were very impressive in a physical battle which had a lot of emotion last weekend against Tonga and we know we are in for a tough contest on Sunday night," Walters said.

"It's going to be a great occasion in front of a full house at Allianz Stadium, and we've got to meet the occasion with our best performance of the tournament."

Samoa have made just one enforced change with Ronald Volkman replacing Chanel Harris-Tavita (hamstring) at five-eighth.

In the other semi-final, Tonga are unchanged while Crossland remains an option to feature for the first time since his four-match suspension for his leg-breaking tackle on Nathan Cleary in the NRL preliminary final.

The Newcastle hooker was officially elevated to New Zealand's squad on Monday night after forward Jacob Laban was ruled out with injury.

Jones has named Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad on the wing as a result of Ronaldo Mulitalo's one-game ban for a shoulder charge against Fiji.

stories.headline: How the NFL trade deadline went from quiet to exciting over the past decade
stories.summary: There were eight trades on deadline day in 2025, a long way from the zero we saw in 2015. We asked execs and agents what set off this big NFL trade deadline boom.
stories.body:
It's NFL trade season, and activity is booming more than at any time in league history. There have been 60 trades this calendar year through October, the fourth most since at least 1990 and nearly double the annual average between 2007 and 2016, per ESPN Research. And we can expect things to get even spicier over the next week with teams wheeling and dealing ahead of the trade deadline at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 10.

Executives I talk to believe we will see double-digit trades between now and the deadline. The skillet is already scorching hot and full of grease -- we've had seven in-season deals. The Bears' all-in move to land defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons last week shows us fewer and fewer players are truly off limits. So ... stay close to your phone.

"I don't talk with other general managers much about it, but it's like an unspoken understanding of this new generation of GMs. We're going to make trades," Bills general manager Brandon Beane said. "People have been more creative. Pick swaps have allowed more opportunity."

For many years, the NFL trade deadline was a non-event snoozer. In 2015, there were no deadline-day trades and just one deadline-week deal. The yearly average between 2010 and 2016 was one player trade per deadline day and fewer than three trades during deadline week. Fast-forward a decade, and we had eight deadline-day trades and 14 deadline-week deals in 2025. In fact, there were at least six trades on deadline day in each of the past four seasons. Prior to that, there were never more than five.

"The old-school way of thinking was more anti-trade," one NFC assistant general manager said. "Now people are much more open to how they add talent to their teams."

General managers couldn't identify the exact moment trade movement took off, though. Two executives pointed to the 2018 Khalil Mack deal, when the edge rusher was traded from the Raiders to the Bears -- but that was in September. One former general manager noted the October 2019 pre-deadline deal in which the Jaguars sent Jalen Ramsey to the Rams for a package that included two first-round picks. L.A. won the Super Bowl two years later, and GM Les Snead wore a "F--- them picks" shirt at the parade that became the mantra for contenders going all-in via trade. Halloween 2017 serves as a key marker, too. The Dolphins traded running back Jay Ajayi to the Eagles, and the Patriots dealt quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo to the 49ers.

No matter which deal sprang the door open, the NFL deadline now rivals the NBA and MLB deadlines in activity and excitement. What happened? What caused this quick change? I spoke with a dozen high-ranking front office executives (including several general managers) and three player agents to dive into the when and why behind this trade deadline boom. Three reasons emerged.

Reason No. 1: Less patience, more deals
There were 10 head coach changes in the 2026 offseason, representing nearly a third of the league and serving as a crystal-clear sign to the rest that they need to win or else. Simply put, fear leads to action.

"There's no more patience. Coaches are getting fired one-and-done. It's so much pressure to win quickly," one AFC high-ranking front office executive said. "You don't have the luxury to wait around to see if a player can figure it out. They are going to move on from you before you get your guys built up. So, let's go get a guy."

From 2017 to 2025, there was an average of 3.6 trades per season involving first- or second-team All-Pro players, per ESPN Research. Teams are more willing to deal significant draft capital for the perceived "missing piece." A couple of All-Pros moved last year on deadline day. The Colts sent two first-round picks to the Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner, trying to maximize their 7-2 start. The Jets traded defensive tackle Quinnen Williams to the Cowboys, who were 3-5-1 and trying to get back on track.

Of course, Indianapolis and Dallas both missed the playoffs after going a combined 5-11 post-deadline. As Beane said, "You're never one player away. ... If you told me trading for a player gave me a 95% chance to win it, then we do it. You don't get that."

Not every in-season deal works out, and Jaguars GM James Gladstone even mentioned that shifts in locker room dynamics can be unintended side effects of trades. Ahead of last year's deadline, Gladstone made a CB-for-CB swap, sending Tyson Campbell to Cleveland for Greg Newsome II. The move made sense for Jacksonville from a schematic and long-term perspective, but Gladstone wondered if the Jaguars' ensuing two straight losses before the bye had something to do with losing Campbell: "It requires a lot more energy to deal with drastic locker room changes."

Still, more NFL teams have put all their chips in, deciding they're willing to give up premium first- and second-round picks to get a difference-maker. From 2012 to 2016, there was an average of 13.8 trades involving first- or second-round picks per year, according to ESPN Research. Over the past five years (since 2022), that average has jumped to 20.4 per year.

"I've been in situations where negative social media chatter from media or fans increases pressure on the coach and GM. It impacts decisions. It 1,000% does," one assistant general manager said. "It's the owners putting pressure on you, too. Owners read it every day on Twitter and sometimes listen to it more than the people they work with day-to-day.

"You must be more aggressive because you don't have five years to figure it out. Twenty years ago? General managers knew they'd get five to eight years for sure, so they acted differently."

Reason No. 2: Growing power for the players
Front offices also feel the pressure from players in today's NFL.

"Guys are more educated on the business side and their strength, compared to earlier years," said one prominent NFL agent who has helped multiple star players get traded. "At the same time, it's a case-by-case situation. Just because one guy can easily get traded doesn't mean it happens as easily for the next guy. Trust and respect between player, agent and general manager are key."

At the end of September, the Cowboys traded for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. after a long contract standoff with the Steelers. It became public that he didn't feel valued in Pittsburgh, as the two sides failed to agree on an extension that satisfied him in terms of guaranteed money. Porter sat out training camp, the preseason and the Steelers' first three games with a back injury that multiple executives said they believe was basically a hold-in strategy. And while Porter didn't have to explicitly say "pay me or trade me" like others, his stance was clear. The saga screamed "Come get Porter" to teams needing help at cornerback.

"Nothing is secret anymore. Back in the day, you could calm down issues internally," Beane said. "But with social media and media 24/7, you can see players' raw emotions in real time. I've made calls on players who looked unhappy based on something that came out publicly."

Colts receiver Josh Downs requested a trade last week, and he could be the next starter out of Indianapolis after the team dealt defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and guard Quenton Nelson. Eagles guard Landon Dickerson appeared to express disconnect with the team's front office on his long-term future, too. Multiple execs told me they are eagerly awaiting clarity on whether the Eagles will be open to dealing several of their intriguing veterans.

"I've never called a GM to say we want to get traded and they immediately say 'yes.' They always say they don't want to trade [the player]. I try to help GMs realize that [they] don't want to have major distractions," one longtime agent said. "I have been in situations where pressure was applied without having to take it publicly."

Another agent added: "I always want the GM to feel like he's really driving the bus. I don't want them to be embarrassed. I want to show him the value he's getting whether it's trade value vs. production or not having to deal with a headache. Some people's hand you can't force. We're dealing with humans. Some people act or don't act on impulse or emotion."

Reason No. 3: More salary cap maneuverability
Browns general manager Andrew Berry made the biggest splash of the offseason by dealing Myles Garrett to the Rams in large part to, as he said, "maximize the salary cap" in a world of skyrocketing salaries for star players.

"You think about it like we get three or four good players and $20-30 million saved from trading Myles," Berry said. "Now, you're giving up a great player in Myles. We think that's worth it."

The Titans used similar thinking this past week, dealing a great player in Simmons with the hopes that the two first-round picks they acquired and eventual cap savings will net them five or six good young players in the years to come. Simmons, now 29 years old in Year 9 of his NFL career, might not still be a prime player once Tennessee is finally ready to compete in 2028-29.

"We know that we have to be better this year, next year, the year after," Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi said. "This draft capital gives us the opportunity. We have a lot of work to do."

Since the salary cap was created in 1994, it has grown from $34.6 million to $301.2 million. It took 15 years to go from $100 million to $200 million. But it took only four years to go from $200 million to $300 million. The average annual cap increase over the past five years is about 10.6%. That matters. The higher salary cap means teams can be more aggressive adding star veterans with more room to pony up for their salaries.

"It doesn't work like fantasy football. If you and I trade players in fantasy, it doesn't impact these players' lives at all," Beane said. "When I trade for a player, there's how much money he makes, how much is the trading team eating, what is his long-term contract, can he learn the playbook, system, signals in time. It doesn't always translate."

Beane recalled his October 2024 pre-deadline trade for receiver Amari Cooper as a perfect example. The Bills were looking for an impact receiver but were very limited in cap space. Cooper was due $20 million that season, a number Buffalo couldn't afford. But the Browns converted most of that money into a salary bonus that made him more obtainable and therefore more costly in trade compensation.

"People publicly questioned why we gave up a third-round pick for Cooper but not a second-round pick for Davante Adams," Beane said. "I couldn't afford Davante salarywise, and there was no salary-cutting option available. So for Amari, it would have been fourth- and sixth-round picks, but since Cleveland ate $10-plus million, we raised our compensation up to a third and sixth."

Ultimately, Cooper made some impact on the offense, but it wasn't seen a lot on the stat sheet and certainly was not as big as expected at the time. Buffalo limited Cooper's playbook to make a complete midseason scheme shift digestible, and he didn't play in key two-minute drills. Over the second half of the season, Cooper had 20 catches for 297 yards and two touchdowns.

Is the trade deadline boom here to stay?
Several league executives believe this deadline boom is just getting started, and the numbers support that observation. Deadline-week trades have occurred five times more frequently this decade compared with the previous decade.

"Analytics have certainly played a key role. Decision-makers are smarter with more info," Berry said. "Positional value has larger priority, and we have so much more information overall on other teams and players."

Information is king. Beane described the wave of younger staffers in NFL teams' analytics departments as an asset. Their expertise using advanced technology and AI gives general managers a lot of data and trade comparisons to guide their decision-making. As Gladstone said, "The industry is getting younger in thought and more creative in building. You must be aware of trends and teams that think similarly to you."

Funny enough, Gladstone said he doesn't enjoy the trade aspect of the job. "It's not fulfilling to me," he said. "I just want to build rosters."

But trades have become an almost mandatory element of long-term roster-building success. And if recent history is any indication, you should expect more surprises, blockbusters and trade alerts over the next week.

stories.headline: Liverpool's $500m forward line is failing. Can they turn it around?
stories.summary: Liverpool's star-studded, expensively assembled attack has scored fewer Premier League goals this season than Ipswich. That needs to improve immediately.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta described it as "remarkable." His Arsenal side had just beat Liverpool 1-0 to secure their first victory at Anfield in more than 14 years, but there was one element of the Premier League champions' performance that appeared to please their manager more than any other.

For the first time on record (since 2003-04), Liverpool had failed to record a shot on target at home in the Premier League, with Gunners goalkeeper David Raya enjoying a surprisingly uneventful afternoon on Merseyside.

"I didn't know about that statistic, but that's incredible," Arteta said in his postmatch news conference. "It didn't feel like this to be fair on the pitch because there were very little margins sometimes when they had the opportunity to shoot and it's a team that shoots a lot. You have to be so good at blocking shots and preventing those spaces for them to get into there.

"Again, it's a commitment of every single player in every action consistently to deliver those kind of stats and to do it against this team, it's something remarkable I would say."

- Arsenal get big win at Liverpool, one Iraola & Co. can learn from

- Arteta, Alonso, Iraola: Three top managers all come from one tiny club

- Ex-Liverpool star Milner runs NYC Marathon in just over three hours

Arteta's assessment was fair. While Liverpool did not do enough to test Raya, they didnpose problems for the Arsenal defence. After falling behind to a Kai Havertz goal in the 16th minute, the hosts pinned the Gunners' back and played with an intensity reminiscent of Jürgen Klopp's "heavy-metal" Liverpool sides.

The Reds had 28 touches in their opponents' penalty area in the first half -- the most on record (since 2008-09) by any team in the opening period of a Premier League game against Arsenal -- and could have been awarded a penalty for Jurriën Timber's shirt pull on Alexander Isak inside the box. Florian Wirtz later hit the crossbar with a free-kick, while Alexis Mac Allister ought to have done better with a header he put over the bar.

However, the fact remains that Liverpool are still not consistently functioning as a fluid attacking unit. They have scored just four goals at Anfield in the Premier League this season, their joint-fewest after five home matches in a top-flight campaign (also four in 1913-14 and 2012-13). In three of their five home league games this term -- against Fulham, Manchester City and now Arsenal -- the Reds have failed to find the back of the net.

So why is their star-studded attack struggling to deliver? And how can manager Andoni Iraola get them back on track?

Big guns not firing
Going into Sunday's game, the matchup was pitched in some quarters as attack vs. defence. The absence of Bukayo Saka plus question marks over the fitness of Noni Madueke and Christos Tzolis had left Arsenal looking shorn of quality up front, while Liverpool's forwards had appeared to be finding their feet during a run of five straight wins in all competitions.

Before the weekend, Isak had scored six goals in his last seven league appearances and had scored in three consecutive games for the first time in more than 18 months. Summer signing Bradley Barcola had registered five goal contributions in four games, while Wirtz had begun to look quietly impressive in the No.10 role.

After Liverpool spent a combined total of £354 million ($462 million) to sign that trio over the past three transfer windows, there was optimism that Liverpool's big guns were beginning to fire on all cylinders just in time to inflict some damage on the reigning champions. In reality, none of the three were able to produce a moment of magic against Arsenal. Adding in Cody Gakpo's £37 million ($49 million) signing in 2023, Liverpool first-choice attacking quartet cost them more than $500 million.

Not for the first time this season, Wirtz was substituted while his team were in need of a goal, ending the afternoon with an expected assists value of just 0.06. Barcola's influence waned after a promising spell in the first half, while Isak enjoyed just 26 touches and completed 12 of his 16 passes.

While Arsenal deserve credit for the robustness of their defence, Liverpool just aren't scoring, or even creating, enough chances in the Premier League. Having scored just 63 league goals under Arne Slot last term -- their lowest tally since 2015-16 -- there has not yet been a significant uptick in that department under Iraola.

Liverpool have scored 11 goals in nine top-flight games this season, two less than newly-promoted Ipswich Town and only one more than Michael Carrick's faltering Manchester United side. In terms of big chances created, the Reds are also performing poorly and currently rank 19th in the league with seven. Comparatively, the best-performing team by that metric, Manchester City, have created 32.

The concern for Iraola will be that Liverpool's stats are actually down from last season. After the same number of games in 2025-26, they had created 24 big chances (ranking second in the league behind City).

There has been a similar decline in other attacking metrics, with the Reds having completed 90 passes into the penalty area this term, down from the 115 they managed in nine games last season. The number of carries ending in the attacking penalty area has also dropped from 167 in 2025-26 to 137 in 2026-27.

Champions League form not translating domestically
It has been a different story in the UEFA Champions League, where Liverpool have scored 12 goals across their three games this season.

"I don't really know the reason," Iraola said last month when quizzed on why his side are more prolific in Europe. "It's true that the LASK game is different, but against Villarreal and Atlético Madrid, I think we've been offensively, especially, really good.

"In the Premier League, we are not scoring at this level and also we are probably defending better. They are different kind of games and different kind of opposition, I think more than [the difference being] the competitions, it is who you have played against."

Admittedly, Liverpool have had a favourable draw in the Champions League this term, but it's clear several of their players feel far more comfortable playing in European competition than they do domestically.

In a recent interview with French outlet Téléfoot, Barcola acknowledged that the Premier League is "less technical" than Ligue 1 and a big step up physically. It is no coincidence, then, that he and Wirtz in particular thrive when they are not having to contend with the intense physical demands of the English game.

Enduring issues in other areas of the pitch are not helping Liverpool up front. Iraola is still searching for the right balance in midfield and boldly handed teenager Trey Nyoni his first league start against Arsenal. After a few nervy moments and heavy tackles in the opening exchanges, the 19-year-old excelled as the Reds' deepest-lying midfielder, with his tally of 53 completed passes and 14 line-breaking passes the most of any player during his 59 minutes on the pitch. While his minutes will need to be managed as he adjusts to a more prominent role in the first-team squad, his development could prove vital in helping to better platform Liverpool's attackers.

There is also much for Iraola to ponder in terms of his full-backs. Milos Kerkez is full of endeavour, but his quality on the ball is a hindrance at times. On the other flank, the addition of Barcelona loanee Ronald Araújo has helped to shore up Liverpool's defence, but his natural instincts as a centre-back means he has limitations offensively.

Ultimately, this iteration of Liverpool is a work in progress. Sources told ESPN that Iraola's propensity for improving attacking players was one of the main reasons for his appointment, but he is just 14 games into his Anfield career and while some of the early signs have been promising, it will take time for him to fully realise his vision.

The 44-year-old coach will also hope that the expected return of France international Hugo Ekitike from an Achilles injury in the coming months can equip his squad with some additional firepower.

"Some days it feels like we are at the top, and some days it feels like we are not even close," midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai told Viaplay after Sunday's game. "It takes time to be at the top, I think."

It was an astute appraisal. Iraola's Liverpool are at the beginning of their journey. How quickly they reach their destination depends on whether his expensively assembled front line can begin delivering on their potential.

stories.headline: Colorado brings 3-game win streak into matchup against Columbus
stories.summary: Colorado Avalanche (9-5-1, in the Central Division) vs. Columbus Blue Jackets (5-7, in the Metropolitan Division)
stories.body:
Colorado Avalanche (9-5-1, in the Central Division) vs. Columbus Blue Jackets (5-7, in the Metropolitan Division)


Columbus, Ohio; Tuesday, 7 p.m. EST

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli overcame George Russell, Ferrari to become F1's youngest champion
stories.summary: How Kimi Antonelli overcame early setbacks, teammate George Russell and a Ferrari fightback to become Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli was crowned the 2026 Formula 1 world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix, sealing the title with four races of the season remaining.

He stood on the last step of the podium, behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton in the Ferrari.

At 20 years old, Antonelli made his title fight look remarkably easy. He laid down the foundations with his maiden victory at the second race of the season in China, and with the exception of the occasional reliability setback with his Mercedes, he remained composed ever since.

It marked Mercedes' return to the top winning its first drivers' and constructors' trophy since Hamilton six years ago, and the team have well and truly unlocked their next superstar -- a superstar simply just enjoying himself.

Here are the highs -- and few low points -- that shaped his title-winning campaign.

- Kimi Antonelli makes F1 history as youngest world champion with maiden title

- Kimi Antonelli's historic F1 title: Every record broken and milestone reached

- In pictures: The moments that defined Kimi Antonelli's F1 title-winning season

Melbourne crash, early favourite Russell wins opener
It was George Russell, not Antonelli, who was the name on everyone's lips coming into the season. Russell was one of the standout performers in 2025, while Antonelli's rookie season had been a rollercoaster. When it was clear Mercedes was the team to beat, Russell was the easy pick for the title.

By the time the season-opener had arrived in Melbourne, it was clear he had finally got what he dreamt of after a tedious four-year wait -- a fast and dominant Mercedes to match his ambition. It was an opportunity he couldn't afford to waste.

To anyone who had paid attention to 2025, it was perhaps not surprising how the opening weekend went. Antonelli showed flashes of pace but a crash in final practice left him on the back foot going into qualifying. TV cameras showed Toto Wolff and his race engineer Peter Bonnington comforting a disconsolate Antonelli after the smash.

Russell claimed pole, although Mercedes' quick repair job allowed Antonelli to get out and lock out the front row of the grid. The race was a showcase of F1's new era. F1's 2026 hybrid engine regulations featured a near 50/50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, but it was instantly met with driver criticism with Max Verstappen labelling them "anti-racing."

At the start of the race, Russell powered down to Turn 1 in a comfortable lead, but a sluggish start for Antonelli followed -- something that would be an early theme of his season. He quickly fought back through the order. A thrilling back and forth contest followed, as Ferrari briefly fought Mercedes for the win, but by the end it was as they were at the beginning -- Russell winning, although he had not been able to shake Antonelli, who finished just under three seconds behind.

Russell seemed overjoyed at the start.

"I love this car, I love this engine!" Russell declared over the radio after the race.

As for Antonelli, the young Italian had managed to avoid the disaster of his practice crash, but he was still tellingly hard on himself afterwards. To team boss Wolff, it was the kind of baptism by fire he expected the Italian would have in his sophomore season now the team was the benchmark car to beat.

"He's literally learning [F1] the hard way, which makes him stronger," Wolff commented on Antonelli after the race. "He was very, very strong on Friday and his pace on Saturday was there. But then the accident happened, and that can happen."

But anyone who thought the opening race of the season was a sign of things to come was gravely mistaken.

Championship standings after Australia:

Russell -- 25

Antonelli -- 18

China breakthrough changes everything
Mercedes showed the first glimpses of vulnerability in China with a series of front wing and technical problems, but it was not enough to stop another lockout of the front row. This time, Antonelli did not repeat any of his Melbourne mistakes, claiming a resounding first career pole position -- becoming the youngest driver in history to do so.

Antonelli had another sluggish getaway though, and after trying to cover Russell into Turn 1, the Mercedes drivers both allowed Hamilton's Ferrari to swoop into an early lead. Mercedes' strong pace quickly showed itself and Antonelli got back ahead a lap later, the beginning of a dominant and assured drive to his first win. It made him F1's second youngest winner of all time, behind Verstappen.

"I'm speechless," an emotional Antonelli said after the race. "I'm about to cry, to be honest. Thank you so much to my team, because they helped me to achieve this dream."

For anyone who had already handed Russell the title after Melbourne, Antonelli's Shanghai drive seemed to be a clear reminder the Brit would not have it all his own way.

It had been a monumental weekend for Antonelli with landmark pole and wins. A week later, he did the same again and took pole at the Japanese Grand Prix, with Russell nearly three-tenths behind. Again, Antonelli struggled at the start, dropping to sixth by the end of the first lap as Oscar Piastri and Charles Leclerc battled for the lead, with Russell fourth. The pendulum of the race seemed to be swinging back to Russell as he carved through the field, but a pit stop on lap 22 from the lead would prove his undoing. Almost immediately afterwards, Oliver Bearman crashed at Spoon, triggering a safety car.

It was manna from heaven for Antonelli, who effectively got a free pit stop, vaulting him up the order and ahead of Russell and Piastri.

"Unbelievable!" said Russell on his radio immediately afterwards.

Russell dropped to fourth by the end, a quite remarkable outcome for such a dominant car. Out in front, Antonelli surged clear, winning over Piastri by a dominant 17 seconds. Antonelli might have been fortuitous getting to the lead, but there was nothing lucky about the margin of victory: Antonelli was looking every bit worthy of his newest accolade and the youngest man to ever lead the world championship. Little did anyone know it then, but it was a lead he would never relinquish.

He would have several weeks to dwell on the new place in the history books, too, with the outbreak of war in Iran cancelling April's races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.

Championship standings after Japan:

Antonelli -- 72

Russell -- 63

Three wins that broke Russell's challenge
The next three races underlined Antonelli's superiority and marked what would be the turning point in the season. Russell was no longer the established team leader waiting for the next generation to catch up -- Antonelli was in fact fully caught up. After the break caused by the Middle East cancellations -- Bahrain was subsequently moved to Malaysia in September -- Russell looked to fight back in Miami and the sprint appeared to suggest the title battle would swing back and forth. Antonelli out-qualified Russell comfortably but his Achilles heel from the year quickly re-emerged as he fluffed his start and dropped down the order. Norris and Piastri claimed a McLaren one-two while Russell was fourth and Antonelli sixth.

The momentum would swing again hours later. In qualifying again the difference between the pair was clear as Antonelli romped to his third straight pole position, with Russell languishing down in fifth. The young Italian's race start got the better of him once again and he ran wide at Turn 1 while Leclerc took a comfortable lead.

Antonelli and Leclerc fought out in front before Norris came into the mix and headed the field on lap 14. It was Antonelli vs. Norris for the rest of the race, before the Italian fended off the reigning world champion to take his third win in a row.

"This is just the beginning," Antonelli declared afterwards. "The road is still long, but we're working super hard and the team is doing an incredible job."

Canada followed and would deliver a blockbuster moment between the Mercedes duo. It was a Russell stronghold -- three pole positions to his name and a victory the year prior, the perfect place to kick life into his stuttering campaign. Russell started perfectly, taking a comfortable sprint pole, with Norris ahead of Antonelli in third. The mini-race featured a tense battle between the pair, with Antonelli being forced wide while trying a very ambitious move around the outside at Turn 1.

The Italian driver would then lose second after going wide a lap later while trying to pass Russell, losing second to Norris. Antonelli was fuming on the radio, leading to an intervention from Wolff. "Kimi, concentrate on the driving please, and not on the radio moaning," he said. Russell knew this weekend was his time to shine and he ended up stamping his authority and producing another stunning pole, but the race couldn't have gone any worse.

Both Mercedes drivers had a poor start while Norris took the lead before being called into the pits. Antonelli and Russell had fierce wheel-to-wheel battles for the best part of 27 laps, providing some excellent entertainment. Neither driver was willing to give an inch -- it seemed like all of Mercedes' worst nightmares coming back to life, with memories of Hamilton and Nico Rosberg's collisions in 2014 and 2016 while fighting each other for championships.

Fate would intervene before Russell and Antonelli were able to create another, with Russell retiring from the lead with a reliability issue while fending off his younger teammate. "It feels like the gods don't want me to be in this fight," a deflated Russell would say later. Antonelli's win rubbed salt into the wounds.

The Brit needed a clean weekend at the Monaco Grand Prix, but instead the problems continued. He qualified in sixth while Antonelli started on pole at a circuit where overtaking is notoriously difficult.

Monaco felt like a sucker punch to Russell. This time, Antonelli was flawless, taking a great pole. Antonelli's launch off the line was strong, but chaos unfolded behind him. In a race filled with incidents, Safety Cars and a red flag. Russell would be one of the drivers given a drive-through penalty for a minor pit-lane speeding infraction -- one later revealed to have been caused by the FIA incorrectly measuring pit entry. During a red flag, Russell argued his penalty should be deferred to after the race, but he served the drive-through anyway, dropping to the back.

Antonelli's win gave him another unanswered 25 points -- 50 in two races. While Canada had shown the raw side of Antonelli, Monaco had shown his class. Russell's championship hopes were slowly slipping from his grasp.

Championship standings after Monaco:

Antonelli -- 156

Russell -- 88

Ferrari fightback puts Antonelli under pressure
A team in red decided to join the title party and arrived to the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix with its first major upgrade -- and suddenly Mercedes had a title challenger.

Russell responded to his title struggles with pole, while Hamilton split the two Mercedes' to start the race second. A perfectly executed three-stop strategy played into the seven-time world champion's hands to make history and win his first race with the Scuderia, becoming the first driver of the season to end Mercedes' winning streak.

Antonelli suffered an electrical shutdown and was forced to retire from second place with just four laps remaining, while Russell gained some much-needed points in the title race. Hamilton cut the gap in the championship to Antonelli by 41 points -- making him a worthy title contender.

Antonelli lost 18 points in the championship and was downcast afterwards. He said: "I feel very empty emotionally right now, because we're trying to soak in what has just happened."

Russell arrived to Austria ready to fight back and locked out the front-row in what was a controversial pole position which occurred during a yellow flag period. He converted his pole into his second race win by nearly three-tenths from Antonelli, who stood on the final spot of the podium.

There might have been a glimpse of hope for Russell who said afterwards that he was "feeling like himself again." But that euphoric feeling was followed by a kick in the teeth at the next race when Antonelli bounced back at the British Grand Prix. He edged out Hamilton to win the sprint race after making a move on lap 8 of 17 from second. He crossed the line 2.7 seconds clear of Hamilton, with Norris third and Russell fourth.

The Italian took his form into the rest of the weekend with a stunning pole ahead of Leclerc. But during the race, it was the Ferrari man who had a mighty launch off the line to take the lead and win his first race in two years.

For Antonelli it was a race to forget as he scrambled for a point in ninth and desperately pleaded on the Mercedes team radio to stay out on track to seal a singular championship point. He was then demoted to 16th following a time penalty for exceeding track limits when he was struggling with car reliability.

It was a mixed bag of results for Mercedes, while Ferrari continued to build momentum. With the summer races in full swing, the championship fight was far from over.

Championship standings after Silverstone:

Antonelli -- 179

Russell -- 154

Hamilton -- 147

Antonelli strikes back

Russell's fightback did not last long. At Spa-Francorchamps, Antonelli got things back on track, claiming pole with a scintillating lap 0.3 seconds quicker than Norris in second, while Russell had to settle for fourth. The first lap seemed to be another of the micromoments which summed up Russell's year. Already starting down on Antonelli, Russell's electrical boost did not materialize in time for the Eau Rouge/Kemmel Straight on the opening lap.

Starved of power, Russell was swallowed up by other cars into Les Combes, tangling with Hamilton's Ferrari and ending in the gravel. "I'm out," Russell said on radio immediately after finishing. "What the f--- happened down the straight? I had no battery down the straight! Unacceptable! Unf------g acceptable!" If there was ever a radio message which summed up his mood and his season, Russell had delivered it. All of his hard work of the past handful of races, the gentle chipping away at Antonelli, was undone like that. Out in front, Antonelli briefly lost the lead to Verstappen, but soon got himself back in front to romp home to another comprehensive win.

Russell's engine issues would emerge again at the start of the Hungarian Grand Prix, as he struggled to get away and dropped from the third row of the grid to the back of the field. Out in front, McLaren's Norris capitalized on teammate Piastri's late race retirement to win.

Going into the summer break, Hamilton appeared to be just as big a threat to Antonelli's championship as Russell.

Championship standings after Belgium:

Antonelli -- 204

Hamilton -- 159

Russell -- 154

Forza Kimi!

Formula 1's summer break ended with the last Dutch Grand Prix to be held at Zandvoort under its current deal. Russell came into the second half of the season promising an all-or-nothing approach to his teammate's title lead and took sprint pole and then sprint victory to kick the season off in positive form.

The pendulum would swing back Antonelli's way the following day. Antonelli got the jump on Russell at the start before Verstappen crashed uncharacteristically on a wet-dry track. Antonelli briefly got ahead of Norris at the restart, but soon dropped behind the McLaren driver again. A late Virtual Safety Car gave Mercedes a dilemma. Antonelli pitted for fresh tyres to cover the threat of the looming Ferrari drivers, but rejoined behind Russell, who had stayed out on older tyres. Antonelli was quicker but also being caught by the two Ferraris. Mercedes immediately intervened, asking Russell to let Antonelli by into second position. Russell would oblige, despite a muted objection on the radio, and held off Hamilton to complete a double podium for Mercedes. It was odd to see a driver move over for a title rival, but showed how well Mercedes had managed the intra-team dynamic.

Rather than it becoming a controversy, Russell defended the call post-race. He said: "I mean, Kimi was ahead of me anyway. He deserved to finish ahead ... That's always just been our sort of rules, and the fact is Kimi was ahead of me before the VSC [Virtual Safety Car], and he tried something different to, you know, protect us as a team."

The Mercedes call was a stark contrast to the Ferrari team, who at a key moment earlier in the race had dithered on asking Leclerc to move over to let Hamilton past, when the seven-time world champion was on a better strategy. Hamilton later argued it cost them a podium finish, at least. It suggested a team not all pulling in one direction -- and the tensions at F1's red team would explode into full public view one week later at Monza.

Antonelli's home Italian Grand Prix promised a moment of real jeopardy. Issues earlier in the season meant he needed a new engine and the back-of-the-grid penalty that came with it. Russell took a resounding pole position ahead of the two Ferrari drivers and it very much seemed game-on: yet another chance for Russell to try and change the momentum of the season, on Antonelli's home patch no less.

But Ferrari came into the race with bitterness lingering from Zandvoort. During qualifying at Monza, Hamilton -- the driver with the best mathematical shot at beating Antonelli -- had felt he was not given priority when it came to qualifying strategy. "The team was solely focused on trying to get an equal tow for each driver," Hamilton said, referring to the Monza trick of one driver giving his teammate an aerodynamic boost by doing a qualifying lap a certain distance ahead.

Hamilton continued: "We're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed. So yeah, we do have to work as a team. But have we been?" Hamilton then shrugged and shook his head, adding: "If and when that will ever change, we'll find out."

It seemed to be a clear plea from Hamilton for Ferrari to back him over Leclerc to try and wrestle the initiative back from Antonelli and Mercedes. Hamilton would get his answer in resounding fashion at Turn 1, when he got on the inside of Leclerc's car on the right-left first chicane. Leclerc refused to budge, pushing Hamilton wide and into the gravel. At the end of the second lap, Leclerc lost control of his car and crashed out. It was the most Ferrari of farces and appeared to end any chance the team had of making the rest of 2026 a two-team fight.

Antonelli's car, equipped with the new engine, was a rocketship. He was carving through the field, with each pass leading to a louder roar from the home crowd. He eventually caught Russell -- who had driven flawlessly out in front -- and, after one botched attempt at getting by which almost ended in the gravel -- Antonelli got ahead for a famous and emotional win, the first by an Italian at the Italian Grand Prix since 1966. Antonelli's 26 passes were the most recorded by a single driver at any race in F1 history. New engine or not, Antonelli had turned in the most magnificent of drives, dealt another bitter blow to Russell, and all while Ferrari fumbled a golden opportunity to give Mercedes some anxiety about a two-team fight. In a season of big moments, Monza was the moment.

As he stood on top of the podium, Antonelli soaked it all in. "The weekend itself was absolutely incredible," Antonelli said later. "Definitely so far the best day of my life, and an incredible memory. I couldn't wish for a better day." Two weeks later at Madrid's first-ever Spanish Grand Prix, Antonelli inched even closer to the title, as Norris' hopes of a win were undone by an awfully timed Safety Car. Antonelli would inherit the lead and keep Norris behind with a faultless drive under pressure to win Madring's processional debut event. Russell could only finish fifth.

Championship standings after Madrid:

Antonelli -- 292

Russell -- 211

Hamilton -- 191

Antonelli romps clear

Antonelli's perfect season appeared to hit a momentary roadblock in qualifying for Baku's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where he dragged his front left tyre into the wall at Turn 1. It was a nightmare moment, a rare unforced error, as teammate Russell settled for second behind surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly. To anyone looking for a championship turnaround, there was historical precedent: Piastri's 2025 season had unraveled with unforced errors in Baku 12 months earlier. Was Antonelli about to trigger the same kind of implosion?

Out in front, Russell quickly got himself into the lead and controlled things from there, holding off old foe Verstappen over a tense final set of laps to record his first win since the Austrian Grand Prix. If Saturday had shown a glimpse of the raw side of the young Antonelli, Sunday showed why he was the champion-in-waiting, as he turned in a sensible and decisive drive to fifth, avoiding further drama on Baku's tight and twisty circuit. Russell's win felt important, but Antonelli had avoided a bigger points swing.

Verstappen's Baku performance had suggested a Red Bull resurgence and he confirmed it at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, a race which was as bizarre in name as it was in drama. A deluge before the start delayed the start, before F1's controversial new engines had a software glitch which caused a red flag before the end of the formation lap. When things finally restarted, Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen all traded places, before Verstappen took control of the race late on. As the finish neared, a final, decisive blow to Russell, as his Mercedes engine packed up a handful of laps from the end. Verstappen claimed Red Bull's first win of the year while Antonelli took an unanswered 18 points.

Russell's DNF was doubly costly, and it knocked him to the back of the grid in Singapore's Marina Bay street circuit. As had been the case a week earlier, Verstappen would control proceedings. Leclerc finished second, with Antonelli having a lonely race to third, but it saw him gain again -- Russell could only manage to fight back to ninth. The result meant Antonelli would go to Austin's United States Grand Prix with a slim mathematical chance of getting it done.

Championship standings after Singapore:

Antonelli -- 340

Russell -- 238

Hamilton -- 229

Antonelli gets it done in North America

If Monza a month earlier had been Antonelli's defining moment, Austin would feel like his unofficial coronation. He could claim the title if he won and Hamilton was fifth or lower and Russell was ninth or lower and arrived in Texas with a spring in his step. On Thursday, he seemed calm and relaxed and by Saturday he was in a perfect stride. Red Bull looked strong but Antonelli was on hand to deny them a pole position, delivering a beautiful lap late in Q3 to edge out Verstappen by 0.179 seconds. Hamilton and Russell settled for fifth and sixth on the grid, respectively, and suddenly the unlikely permutations felt a little less farfetched.

Race day came and it felt like Antonelli could get it done. But first he would have to navigate Verstappen -- the Red Bull opting to start on the grippier soft tyre off the line, while Antonelli and Mercedes opted for the medium, teasing a blockbuster run up COTA's hill to Turn 1. But anyone hoping for fireworks would be disappointed. Antonelli moved across to cover Verstappen at the start -- those sluggish getaways of the first part of the year a distant memory. The Italian immediately started building a lead as Verstappen was swallowed into a fight with the two Ferraris and Norris. Antonelli would only briefly surrender the lead in the pit stop phase of the race, but once back out in front he would disappear again, crossing the line 17 seconds clear of the next quickest car.

At one point, the maths made him champion, albeit briefly. Russell's race was hampered by a five-second time penalty, which turned an already poor event into a desperate one, and he soon dropped to ninth at the same point Hamilton was fifth -- exactly what Antonelli needed. By the finish, both had gained an additional place, meaning Hamilton finished fourth and Russell eighth.

Either way, it was a thumping win and felt like his championship affirmation moment. "Yes! That's how we f------ do it," Antonelli said on the radio after taking the chequered flag. "Let's do it."

Wolff felt like it was the standout drive of his young career. "For me, the best race that he's delivered so far," the Mercedes boss said. "Getting off the start with the inferior [medium] tyre and then controlling it at all times. The race of a champion who isn't the champion yet, but exceptional. So I think he's outperformed the car. Maybe it's a bit harsh to say, but I think his driving style just glues with the car."

It meant he needed just two points from the final five races to be champion and he would need to wait just seven days to start the party -- albeit after what he would describe as one of the most difficult weeks of his life.

Calm, jokey and mischievous in Austin, Antonelli arrived in Mexico City tense and unwell. He would miss Thursday's media session, later saying he felt "very bad." He added: "I had a high fever and stomach problems, so it hasn't been easy. But now I feel OK, just low on energy, just feel pretty tired, so it's going to be important to try and sleep well, because I haven't been sleeping well in these days, and hopefully tomorrow I will have more energy."

He clearly was not at 100% when qualifying came and, in a quirky twist on Austin, when his two competitors qualified down the order, they locked out the front row -- Hamilton claimed a spectacular first pole position for Ferrari, with Russell taking second place alongside his former teammate. Antonelli qualified fifth, which became fourth after a grid penalty for Verstappen. "I'm aware that definitely I haven't been driving well," Antonelli said afterwards. "I felt like already going to qualifying, I didn't feel great, and I felt a bit low on energy, so definitely, you know, it's not an excuse, but for sure, it hasn't been my finest performance."

The young Italian's plan to have a good night's sleep ahead of the biggest day of his life? "Bombard myself with melatonin," he said. Antonelli looked like a different man on Sunday, although he took a cautious approach to the start and standing restart that followed mid-race. There was drama ahead, with an clumsy Leclerc move on Hamilton handing Red Bull and Verstappen the win on a silver platter, but Antonelli didn't need to worry about any of it. A decisive move on Leclerc late on got him into the podium places and he spent the final laps of the race watching the two greatest drivers of his lifetime race for the win.

He admitted the view through his visor -- including that of Hamilton's Ferrari -- was getting blurrier as he neared the chequered flag. "[I was] already [crying] the lap before," Antonelli said later. "I think I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying, basically. I couldn't see clearly ahead. You know, I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears."

Antonelli came home third, more than enough to clinch the title, to trigger wild celebrations with his team, and his family, who had flown in overnight from Italy to watch his crowning moment. "I am speechless, trying to process what just happened," Antonelli said later.

"A day I will remember forever. So grateful, thank you so much. I am going to enjoy every bit. I'm going to out with my family, friends and the team and we're just going to enjoy all the way because this is a very special moment and one we will remember forever."

The championship makes Antonelli F1's youngest, aged 20 years and 86 days.

Standings after Mexico City:

Antonelli -- 380

Verstappen -- 261

Hamilton -- 259

Russell -- 250

stories.headline: Fantasy baseball reactions to MLB offseason trades, signings
stories.summary: Track all the latest MLB free agency and trade news with fantasy baseball analysis from Tristan H. Cockcroft and Eric Karabell.
stories.byline: Tristan H. Cockcroft and Eric Karabell
stories.body:
Tracking the offseason MLB trades and signings with fantasy baseball implications for the upcoming season, Eric Karabell and Tristan H. Cockcroft will analyze and provide an outlook for all of the key players involved.

With the World Series now behind us, players will be allowed to sign with new teams beginning Nov. 2, although typically things don't really start to heat up until the league's annual winter meetings. This year's meetings are scheduled to take place in San Diego from Dec. 7-9.

However, as the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, the 2027 season (as well as the financial rules that will govern it), players and teams alike may end up waiting until after the dust settles on negotiations and a potential lockout before inking any new deals.

In any event, as any contracts do get signed or trades get agreed to, this is the place to find all of the fantasy fallout of those deals. Be sure to check back throughout the hot stove season for updates.

Below, you will find a list of some of the top free agents at each position. Players labeled with a (Q) have received a qualifying offer from their current team and have until Nov. 17 to accept the deal or decline and become a free agent. Players coming from Japan/Korea who were posted by their current team have a Dec. 1 deadline to reach a deal with an MLB club in order to play in the United States in 2027.

Note: Not every transaction warrants the attention of fantasy managers, but for those signings and trades that do merit analysis, you'll find them listed below. Players will be separated by position and then listed in chronological order of the move within each positional grouping, with the latest news coming first. Also included are links to any standalone analysis stories and/or videos regarding major free agent signings and trades. Players who end up re-signing with their previous team will not always be included.
